blocks.text: Flaming Head’s answer did not reach her mind quickly enough.
Laura watched his face. The little hope she had allowed herself began to shrink.
“I don't know how to take it away.”
She looked down at the rocks.
“But I can help you learn what it does,” he said. “You shouldn't have to find everything out alone.”
Laura pulled her jacket tighter. “I burned a hole in my sink.”
She told him about the toothpaste, the burning tissue and turning away before she laughed.
Flaming Head listened without interrupting.
When she finished, he stayed at the same distance. Laura had not realized until then that she had been waiting for him to move away.
“You believe me.”
“Yes.”
She took a breath that shook on the way out.
“All right,” she said. “What do I do?”

The following afternoon, she met him at a disused concrete slipway farther along the shore. A gravel patch lay beneath a steep bank of bare earth. They checked the area first, including the path above and the water's edge. There were no boats, dry weeds or people behind the place they chose.
Laura had brought an old metal baking sheet. She stood it against the earth bank, away from the water, and went back to the concrete.
Flaming Head hovered well to one side.
“Start with as little as you can,” he said.
Laura looked at the sheet.
For months, she had tried to keep anything from leaving her mouth. Now somebody was asking her to do it on purpose.
She spat.
An orange streak crossed the space between her and the target. The sheet rang against the bank. A dark spot spread around a tiny glowing hole.
blocks.alt: Civilian Laura spits a small orange plasma shot at a baking sheet backed by an earth bank while Flaming Head observes from the side.

blocks.text: Laura stepped back, then remembered Flaming Head was watching.

It took several attempts. Twice she missed and struck the bare earth. Each time they stopped and checked where the plasma had landed. When someone appeared on the upper path, Laura waited until they were well beyond the practice area before trying again.
By the end, she could put a small shot near the center of the sheet.
She looked at the marks and felt something she had not expected.
She wanted to show someone.
“You chose where it went,” Flaming Head said.
Laura almost smiled. “For once.”
They stayed until the target and the ground had cooled. Laura looked back at the two misses in the earth bank.
“What if that had been somebody’s window?” she asked. “Or somebody standing there?”
“Then we stop. That’s why we’re practicing here.”
“People won’t care that I was practicing. They’ll see what I did and come looking for me.” She pulled at her jacket sleeve. “They could find out where I live.”
Flaming Head drifted nearer. “I gave two others costumes to help keep people from recognizing them. I can do the same for you.”
“Will it make my aim any better?”
“No. We still have to work on that.”
Laura looked down at the sheet, then back at him. “But they wouldn’t see Laura Baxter.”
“A mask can help. It won’t stop anyone who already knows you.”
She took off her glasses and put them in their case beside her coat. Then she gathered her hair into a ponytail. “All right.”
“Stand still. You won’t be hurt.”

Flaming Head swept around her. Golden fire circled her shoulders and spiraled down to her feet. Laura held her breath, but the light felt warm against her skin. It settled into her clothes, then faded to sparks.
A fitted black suit covered her, with red, orange and yellow flames running up its sides. She touched the edge of the black mask around her eyes, then flexed her gloved fingers.
“You can take it off like ordinary clothes,” he said.
Laura bent her knees and lifted her arms. The suit moved with her. She reached for her coat and folded it over one arm.
That evening she stood before her mirror in the costume Flaming Head had given her.
With her hair pulled into a ponytail and the mask fastened, she looked different enough that she kept turning to check. Her glasses lay in their case on the dresser.
blocks.alt: Seen from the side, Laura checks her black eye mask in the bedroom mirror, wearing her flame-sided costume; her glasses and folded everyday clothes rest on the dresser.

blocks.text: At the next practice, she wore the suit beneath her coat. She put her glasses in their case, fastened the mask and folded the coat well clear of the target area.
This time, she stood a little straighter before facing the target.

Her aim was better. She could make the shot smaller when she took her time. Through their private connection, Flaming Head guided her in choosing where to stand, checking what lay beyond a target and knowing when not to use it.
“You might be able to help someone with this,” he told her.
Laura examined the holes in the sheet. A line of them ran close together now.
“Maybe.”

Walking back that afternoon, she kept the mask on. Her coat was open over the suit, and she had rolled the cooled baking sheet in an old towel beneath one arm. She had not used a hero's name. She had not decided she was one.
At a corner newsstand, she stopped beside a rack to look at the front page.
A man behind the counter glanced at the flames on her clothes.
“Something happening?” he asked.
“Not that I know of.”
He smiled. “Let me know if it does.”
Laura reached into her coat pocket for change. The tickle in her nose came so suddenly that she barely had time to recognize it.
Her hand started toward her mouth.
She remembered the tissue and turned away from the man instead.
The sneeze bent her forward.
Bright droplets struck a low stack of newspapers beside the rack.
For a moment, there were only little orange holes. Then the top paper curled, and fire ran beneath it.
Laura dropped the wrapped sheet.
“Move back!”
The seller looked down. He reached for the burning stack, then snatched his hands away as flame climbed the papers behind it.
“Don't touch it!” Laura caught his sleeve and pulled him clear of the counter.
blocks.alt: Masked Laura pulls the newsstand seller away from burning newspapers as a bystander approaches with an extinguisher; her wrapped baking sheet lies on the sidewalk.

blocks.text: He stumbled onto the sidewalk. She went with him, putting herself between him and the stand without knowing what else to do.
“There's someone inside!” a woman shouted.
“No,” the seller said, coughing. “Just me. I'm out.”

A man ran from the shop next door with an extinguisher. Laura pointed to the burning papers and stepped aside for him. White powder struck the rack. The flames dropped, then showed again beneath the counter.
“Call the fire department!” she shouted.
Someone was already running toward a telephone. Laura waved two people away from the far side of the stand.
“Back. Please, farther back.”
The seller kept looking at the fire, then at her mouth.
“That came from you.”
Laura nodded. She could not make herself say anything else.
A camera clicked behind her.

By the time the fire engine arrived, the little stand was burning from the counter to its wooden roof. Laura stood with the seller while firefighters pushed the crowd back. She answered the first questions twice because the man asking could not hear her over the engine.
“No one was inside,” she said. “I pulled him away.”
She pointed to the seller, who stood with another firefighter.
“Are you hurt?” she called to him.
He shook his head. Then he turned back to what was left of his stand.
Laura stayed until the fire was out. Water ran dark along the curb. The painted sign had fallen face down, and wet magazines lay among the blackened boards.
She found her towel and the baking sheet where someone had moved them clear. She picked them up without looking at the holes.
The seller sat on a chair brought from the next shop.
“I'm sorry,” she told him.
He rubbed both hands over his face.
“I don't know what you want me to say.”
She stood beside him a moment longer. Then she stepped away to answer another question.
The next morning, Laura bought a newspaper from a different stand.
She saw the photograph before the headline. There she was in the mask, one arm lifted to keep people back. Behind her, flames rose from the rack.
LAVA LIPS TORCHES NEWSSTAND.
Laura read it again.

The story beneath described a sneeze, frightened witnesses and the seller being pulled clear. No injuries had been reported. A woman quoted near the end said Laura had helped get people away from the fire.
The headline stayed the same.
The seller handed her the change. Laura had put her glasses back on and let her hair hang loose. She folded the photograph inward before leaving.
When Flaming Head found her at the practice place, the baking sheet was still wrapped.
She held up the paper.
“Lava Lips.”
He looked at the photograph, then at her.
“It was an accident,” she said.
“I believe you.”
“I know how to hit the middle of a baking sheet. I can make a little hole or a bigger hole. But I can't stop a sneeze.”
Flaming Head lowered until they were nearer eye level.
“Then we need to work on what happens when you aren't expecting it.”
Laura stared at him.
“Work on it.” She pressed the folded newspaper against her leg. “That’s what you keep saying.”
“Can you give that man his stand back?”
“No.”
“Can you make it safe for somebody to kiss me?”
Flaming Head said nothing.
Laura looked toward the metal target.
“You keep finding things I can do with it. I'm telling you what it's taken from me.”
Laura's eyes filled. She took off her glasses so she could wipe them without smearing the lenses.
“I asked for help,” she said. “I didn't ask you to teach me how to burn things better.”
blocks.alt: Tearful Laura confronts a saddened Flaming Head by the lake, holding her glasses and the folded newspaper, with the baking sheet and towel nearby.

blocks.text: Flaming Head stayed clear of her. This time, the distance made her angrier.
“Laura—”
“Please. Just leave me alone.”
He waited a moment.
“I'll be nearby if you want to talk.”
She turned her face away. When she looked back, he had moved off along the water.
The target stood where they had left it, with sunlight showing through the holes.
Across Cleveland, Daniel Orkleson stopped at the same photograph.
He sat on a bench with the newspaper across his knees and checked the Army demonstration date on the clipping from his pocket.
Luke hovered behind the bench.
“What now?”
Daniel studied the photograph and the bright droplets striking the papers.
blocks.alt: Daniel studies the headline “Lava Lips Torches Newsstand” and its photograph of masked Laura warning bystanders while Luke hovers behind his bench; the Army announcement lies beside him.

blocks.text: “Interesting.”
“A newsstand burned down.”
“I can read.”
“Is that all you're interested in?” Luke asked. “More things getting burned?”
Daniel folded the paper carefully around the photograph.
“Someone ought to find out what she can do.”
